title: Thomas (3 July)
hook: the doubter who, tradition says, took the gospel to India

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first martyrs of Rome, the crowd with no names. Your line was no names, all known. Whose name did you learn? Day one thousand five.

"Doubting Thomas." People say it at work about the colleague who wants to see the numbers, at home about the kid who won't believe the stove is hot. It has stuck to him. But read John's Gospel, and the man who doubts is also the man who, the first time we hear him speak, offers to die. And when he finally believes, what he says about Jesus is startlingly plain. Yesterday, witnesses with no names. Today, a witness with a nickname he might not have chosen. Thomas.
screen: `DOUBTING THOMAS.` → `THE MAN WHO OFFERED TO DIE.` → `STARTLINGLY PLAIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: First scene. Jesus decides to go back toward Judea, where people had tried to stone him, because his friend Lazarus has died. The disciples protest. Thomas, John says, "who is called Didymus," which is Greek for twin, turns to the others: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." Grim, maybe. But brave. Second scene. On the evening of the resurrection day, Jesus appears to the disciples, and Thomas isn't there. They tell him. He refuses to take it secondhand. "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe." That's the line that earned the nickname. Third scene, eight days later. Thomas is with them. Jesus comes, stands among them, and offers Thomas exactly what he asked for: put your finger here, see my hands. John never says Thomas touches him. What he says is: "Thomas answered, and said to him: My Lord and my God." Not teacher. Not prophet. My Lord and my God. Catholics hear in it a full confession of faith in Jesus, and it comes from the man who wouldn't believe secondhand. Jesus answers: blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed. Then the Gospel goes quiet about him. Tradition carries on. It says Thomas went east, preached in India, and died there as a martyr. Some Christians in India, above all the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala, trace their church to him. Historians debate the details. For those churches, the tradition is their own story.
screen: `LET US ALSO GO, THAT WE MAY DIE.` · `UNLESS I SEE, I WILL NOT BELIEVE.` · `HE NEVER SAYS HE TOUCHED.` · `TRADITION: EAST TO INDIA.` · then, large: `MY LORD AND MY GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Christians in India. Let your breathing slow. Bring to mind the churches of India: old communities and new ones, in cities and villages, some of them small and under pressure. Picture a family going to church on a hot morning, in a language you may not know. Hold them. If you pray, you can say Thomas's words, my Lord and my God, slowly, once, and offer them for those communities. If you don't, simply wish them peace and safety. The bell holds the time.
Thomas. The apostle called the Twin, who doubted, then said my Lord and my God, and who, tradition says, carried the gospel to India.
Your line: my lord and my god. Today, when you doubt something, say so honestly, and stay in the room long enough to see. Day one thousand five.

howItsDone: The Church keeps the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle on 3 July; in India, the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala keep it as the feast of the apostle they trace their church to.

original.note: Greek: twin — John's name for Thomas.

trapdoor: what you thought: doubting Thomas, the apostle who failed.
what it means: the brave, blunt apostle whose confession is startlingly plain.
what a scholar hears: John 20:27–28 offers touch but records only speech; the India tradition appears in the Acts of Thomas, and Kerala's Saint Thomas Christians claim him as founder.

notes: 'Who is called Didymus': quoted from John 11:16 in the voice but not listed as a separate quoted source; Douay-Rheims reads 'Thomas therefore, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples'. Confirm.
'Didymus is Greek for twin': a translation gloss, not an etymology; confirm.
'The plainest words about Jesus anywhere in the Gospels' (hook) and 'one of the clearest statements of faith' (teach): superlatives under the claims rule; Keeper may soften or cut.
'The man who doubted the longest': interpretive; confirm or cut.
India tradition: 'tradition says' kept; 'The tradition itself is old' and 'held dearly' unsourced; Keeper to confirm. Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala naming is standard.
howItsDone: 'great devotion' in Kerala; confirm or soften.

Editor: John 20:19 sets the appearance on the evening of the resurrection day, not 'the night after'; 'Christians in India' (all) narrowed to 'some'; quoted 'who is called Didymus' added to sources; howItsDone 'great devotion' claim cut.
Audit: 'going to Mass' changed to 'going to church' (India's churches include Syro-Malabar, Orthodox and Protestant communities, who name their liturgy differently); stock practice opening varied.
